strengths: Addresses a critical limitation of neural ABI: failure on out-of-distribution data due to model misspecification
Theoretically sound: Propositions 1-4 rigorously establish strict properness of self-consistency losses; Proposition 3 shows no trade-off between loss components regardless of p*(x)
Principled approach that leverages Bayesian self-consistency elegantly, avoiding requirement for ground-truth parameters (key advantage over calibration methods)
Impressive empirical results on the tested benchmark: maintains accuracy far beyond training data distributions (Figure 1); standard NPE fails at μ_obs ≥ 2 while proposed method succeeds at μ_obs > 3
Comprehensive ablation studies: Figure 2 systematically varies dimensionality, dataset size, data location, demonstrating robustness of findings across these factors
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-motivated problem statement
weaknesses: Paper explicitly incomplete: Authors state 'still work in progress' and acknowledge missing experiments on multiple model classes, challenging posterior geometries, and high-dimensional scenarios—these are substantial gaps for publication at a top-tier venue

Severely limited experimental scope: Only single benchmark class tested (multivariate Gaussian/normal means problem); no real-world data despite being primary motivation; 'unlabeled' data is still simulated (Eq. 14), not actual real-world observations

No true model misspecification testing: Experiments only vary observation location (mean shift), not actual model misspecification scenarios (wrong likelihood family, missing variables, etc.) that motivated the work
Missing empirical comparisons: No direct comparison with cited related methods (Gloeckler et al. 2023, Ward et al. 2022, Siahkoohi et al. 2023, Wehenkel et al. 2024); only baseline is standard NPE

Critical limitation with estimated likelihood: Figure 3 shows substantial posterior SD bias when likelihood is estimated; strict properness requires known likelihood, and properness is lost when both posterior and likelihood are approximate—a severe practical limitation since true likelihoods are rarely available

Scalability concerns: While D=100 tested, 'very high-dimensional scenarios' listed as future work; method requires fast density evaluations, restricting to normalizing flows and excluding free-form methods (flow matching); modern applications often require 1000+ dimensions

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Choice of proposal distribution p_C(θ) acknowledged as influential but not investigated; loss weighting λ not studied; authors acknowledge empirical consequences of p_C(θ) selection are 'difficult to anticipate'

Theoretical gaps: No finite-sample convergence rates or sample complexity analysis; no characterization of pre-asymptotic behavior; mechanism explaining strong out-of-distribution performance not deeply analyzed
Limited statistical rigor: Figure 2 shows error bars but lacks formal significance testing; number of experimental runs and random seed procedures not specified; reproducibility procedures unclear

Incomplete failure analysis: Degradation when unlabeled data from training distribution (μ*=0) shown but not explained; behavior when unlabeled data far from true distribution untested; failure modes not discussed

Overstated claims: Authors claim 'major breakthrough' and 'remarkable improvements' based on single synthetic problem; statement 'If our findings also generalize...' reveals uncertainty about generalization
Missing code and reproducibility details: No code provided; some architectural choices could be more explicit; hyperparameter selection procedures incomplete

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in the robustness of neural ABI on out-of-simulation data
Provides formal theoretical grounding via Propositions 1-4 establishing strict properness of self-consistency losses
Avoids restrictive assumptions compared to related work (no ground-truth parameters, post-hoc corrections, or architectural modifications)
Thorough ablation studies on the normal means problem across multiple dimensions, dataset sizes, and configurations
Clean semi-supervised and meta-learning framing of the problem
weaknesses: Paper is explicitly unfinished (stated in abstract as 'work in progress') with acknowledged missing experiments on multiple model classes, challenging posterior geometries, and high-dimensional scenarios—this is disqualifying for a top-tier venue
Experimental validation is severely limited to a single toy model (normal means problem) with closed-form posterior—not representative of real inverse problems in practice
Zero empirical comparisons with related robustness-improving methods [16, 35, 37, 38]—only conceptual comparisons provided
Significant performance degradation with estimated likelihoods (SD bias reverses sign, MMD 2-3× larger), which limits practical applicability since real likelihoods are unknown
Limited novelty: self-consistency losses are from prior work [22, 34]; main contribution is applying existing method to unlabeled data, which is relatively straightforward
Clear performance degradation scaling with dimensionality (D=100 shows substantial uncertainty) contradicting claim of 'no major curse of dimensionality'
Critical requirement (unlabeled data must be sufficiently out-of-distribution) is buried rather than highlighted upfront; method fails when μ*=0
No empirical evaluation on true model misspecification—only distribution shift within same model family is tested
Computational cost of variance-based self-consistency loss not analyzed; requires L=32 samples per observation but no training time comparisons provided
Hyperparameter selection for λ is unexplored—no ablation on sensitivity to weighting parameter that balances two loss components
Lacks practical guidance for practitioners: how to choose M (unlabeled dataset size), which out-of-distribution data to collect, which distribution to target
Theoretical results establish properness but not convergence rates or finite-sample bounds; Proposition 2's support assumption may fail in practice with unknown consequences
Uncertain scope of guarantees: properness is lost when both posterior and likelihood are approximate (acknowledged end of Section 2.3), but this is the common case
Results with summary networks (K=10) show concerning SD bias, suggesting limitations in realistic multi-observation settings
No experiments on standard SBI benchmarks despite citations to them, no evaluation on posteriors with challenging geometries (funnels, multimodality, correlations)

strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized limitation of neural ABI: poor robustness on out-of-simulation data
Solid theoretical contributions: rigorous proofs that self-consistency losses are strictly proper (Propositions 1-4), with Proposition 3 showing no trade-off under model misspecification
Clever semi-supervised approach leveraging Bayesian self-consistency without requiring ground-truth parameters, enabling use of unlabeled real-world data
Compelling proof-of-concept results on normal means problem: dramatic improvements in out-of-distribution generalization, with accurate inference far beyond training data
Practical advantages over related work: maintains amortization, requires no post-hoc corrections, ground-truth parameters, or adversarial defenses
Systematic ablation studies (Figure 2) demonstrating robustness across varying parameter dimensionality, dataset sizes, and distribution shifts
Clear presentation of methodology with intuitive motivation from Bayes' rule symmetry
Demonstrates improvements even with minimal unlabeled data (as few as 4 observations)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only single test problem (multivariate Gaussian/normal means) that is relatively simple with conjugate structure and analytical posterior available. No validation on other model classes, realistic simulators, or challenging posterior geometries (multi-modality, correlations, funnels)

Paper explicitly marked as 'work in progress' with acknowledged missing experiments: 'In the full version, we will provide further experiments... for several different model classes from common benchmarks'

No empirical comparison with related robustifying methods: despite extensive related work discussion (Wehenkel et al. [38], Gloeckler et al. [16], Ward et al. [37]), no head-to-head experimental comparisons provided
No validation on real data: all experiments synthetic with controlled distribution shift; central motivation emphasizes real-world applicability but this is not demonstrated

Significant performance degradation with estimated likelihood (Figure 3): substantially larger biases and MMD distances compared to known likelihood case; posterior standard deviation bias becomes problematic

Incomplete theoretical guarantees in practical settings: Propositions 1-2 assume known likelihood; Proposition 4 (estimated likelihood) only provides strict properness when posterior is known; practical case with both approximate posterior and likelihood lacks theoretical guarantee

Critical design choice under-explored: choice of proposal distribution p_C(θ) acknowledged as influential on training dynamics but only one choice empirically tested; sensitivity to hyperparameter λ not explored

Unclear practical guidance for practitioners: method requires unlabeled data 'at least slightly out-of-distribution' (μ* ≥ 1); how to select or generate appropriate unlabeled data in practice is not addressed
Computational overhead not reported: self-consistency loss requires sampling from posterior (L=32 samples per iteration); training cost comparison with alternative robustifying methods missing

Scalability questions: results up to 100D show 'larger discrepancies'; no truly high-dimensional experiments; paper mentions 'very high-dimensional scenarios' as future work, suggesting not yet achieved
Limited novelty: self-consistency losses from prior work [22, 34]; main contribution is combining with unlabeled data, which is incremental
Statistical rigor concerns: inconsistent error bars across results; number of runs and random seeds not clearly stated; high-dimensional variance estimates from L=32 samples potentially unreliable
Variance-based loss may be problematic for multi-modal posteriors where variance is not meaningful quality measure

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in amortized Bayesian inference—robustness to out-of-simulation data
Solid theoretical contributions: Propositions 1-4 rigorously establish strict properness of self-consistency losses, with Proposition 3 showing robustness to model misspecification
Compelling empirical results on tested cases: dramatic improvements over standard NPE, with near-unbiased posterior estimates far beyond training data
Comprehensive ablation studies (dimensionality, dataset size, likelihood specification) demonstrating robustness across multiple factors
Practical method with desirable properties: maintains amortization, requires no ground-truth parameters for unlabeled data, preserves proper Bayesian inference
Effective with minimal unlabeled data: improvements even with M=1 or M=4 unlabeled observations
Clear presentation with good motivation and mathematical exposition
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: only 2 case studies (one synthetic, one real) and 2 model classes; insufficient to support 'major breakthrough' claim

Degraded performance with estimated likelihoods: significantly larger posterior SD bias and MMD when both posterior and likelihood are estimated, but this critical limitation receives only brief acknowledgment
Limited scalability characterization: experiments only up to D=100 (with visible degradation); no demonstration on high-dimensional problems typical in modern applications
Insufficient analysis of when/why the method works: lacks theoretical or systematic empirical characterization of success conditions and failure modes
Methodological novelty is incremental: primarily applies existing self-consistency losses from [38] to the semi-supervised setting; limited architectural or algorithmic innovation
Missing comparisons with other robustness methods: no direct comparison with cited approaches like Wehenkel et al. [42], Gloeckler et al. [19], or Ward et al. [41]
Hyperparameter analysis missing: choice of λ, proposal distribution p_C(θ), and number of samples L not investigated despite acknowledged impact on performance
Overstated claims: 'remarkable improvements' and 'major breakthrough' language seems inflated relative to the limited experimental validation provided
No training time or computational cost analysis reported; code availability not mentioned
Technical assumption in Proposition 2 may not hold in practice: support of p_C(θ) may not encompass support of p(θ|x) early in training

strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized problem in ABI: brittleness on out-of-simulation data due to model misspecification

Theoretically sound: Propositions 1-4 correctly establish that self-consistency losses are strictly proper, with elegant proof that semi-supervised loss remains strictly proper regardless of distribution shift
Novel semi-supervised approach: First to combine self-consistency with unlabeled real-world data without requiring ground-truth parameter labels

Compelling results on toy problem: Normal means case provides clear evidence with analytically available ground truth; dramatic improvement from complete failure of standard NPE to robust estimation far beyond training distribution
Comprehensive ablations on normal model: Systematic study of dimensionality (2-100D), unlabeled dataset size, distribution shift magnitude, and likelihood specification
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: Only 2 case studies (normal means + air traffic); normal means is conceptually simple despite dimensionality; single real-world application insufficient to support claims of 'major breakthrough'

Critical omission: No empirical comparisons to cited robustness methods (Gloeckler et al. [19], Ward et al. [41], Siahkoohi et al. [39], Gao et al. [16], Wehenkel et al. [42]); impossible to assess if improvements are from self-consistency loss or other factors

Significantly weaker performance with estimated likelihood (practical case): Figure 4 shows posterior mean bias 2-3x larger, posterior SD bias reverses sign, and MMD substantially increases when likelihood is estimated; authors acknowledge this as open challenge but don't address it

Missing theoretical understanding: While Propositions 1-3 establish strict properness, paper lacks theoretical analysis of why/when self-consistency improves generalization to OOD data or formal characterization of when method succeeds/fails

Critical dependency on data heterogeneity: Improvements in normal means vanish when unlabeled data matches training distribution (Figure 3); unclear how insights transfer to different OOD regions, suggesting method may require seeing the specific type of shift at test time

Inadequate practical guidance: No ablation on weight λ, no systematic study of proposal pC(θ) despite authors noting empirical consequences are 'difficult to anticipate', no guidance on number of unlabeled samples M needed, no computational cost analysis despite claims of competitive times

Overselling in abstract and discussion: Claims of 'major breakthrough' and 'remarkable improvements' based on 2 case studies exceed what evidence supports; language significantly stronger than justified by experimental validation
Missing statistical rigor: Lack of error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests in key figures; hard to assess whether reported differences are meaningful vs. noise
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned, some implementation details unclear (e.g., sampling procedure for variance computation in Eq. 4)

Incomplete experimental design: Air traffic study only compares to Stan (not other ABI methods); no analysis of failure modes; Figure 1 uses only mean shift not other distributional shifts; high-dimensional results (100D) show degradation but limited discussion

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated practical limitation of ABI methods—poor robustness on out-of-distribution data due to model misspecification or domain shift
Novel semi-supervised approach combining labeled simulated data with unlabeled real data using self-consistency losses without requiring ground-truth parameters
Rigorous theoretical foundation with Propositions 1-4 establishing strict properness of self-consistency losses, particularly elegant result that properness holds for any data distribution p*(x)
Convincing empirical results demonstrating dramatic robustness improvements far beyond training data (e.g., µ_obs > 3 when standard NPE collapses at µ_obs ≥ 2)

Comprehensive experimental validation with well-controlled normal means problem (known ground truth), extensive ablations on dimensionality/dataset size/likelihood, and realistic air traffic case study
Strong practical advantages over prior work: no ground-truth parameters needed, maintains amortization and speed, enables proper Bayesian inference
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating the key contributions
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope: only two application domains tested (normal means and air traffic); broader coverage across different model classes (gravitational waves, epidemiology, etc.) would strengthen generalization claims

Significant performance degradation when likelihood is estimated rather than known (Figure 4), which is problematic for practical applications where likelihoods are typically unknown; posterior SD bias sometimes reverses sign without clear explanation

Insufficient practical guidance on key hyperparameters: choice of proposal distribution p_C(θ) acknowledged to influence training dynamics but not thoroughly explored; weight λ balancing losses has no ablation; number of samples L for variance estimation unjustified
No computational cost analysis provided: overhead of sampling from posterior for variance computation at each training iteration not quantified; claim of maintained speed not empirically verified

Limited failure mode analysis: paper emphasizes successes but provides minimal discussion of when SC loss fails; behavior when µ*=0 shows reduced benefits (Figure 3) only briefly mentioned; unclear what happens with severe model misspecification

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 3 assumes exact optimization with infinite data, but practice involves finite samples and approximate optimization; impact of these approximations on theoretical guarantees unexplored
Missing direct empirical comparisons with cited methods (Wehenkel et al. 2024, Gloeckler et al., Ward et al.) on identical problems to contextualize performance gains
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; no open-source release mentioned despite implementation complexity
Performance degradation at higher dimensions (D=100) shown in Figure 3 suggests scalability concerns despite claims of 'no major curse of dimensionality'
Abstract and conclusion use strong language ('major breakthrough') that may overstate claims given limited experimental scope and unresolved issues with estimated likelihoods

strengths: Addresses important and practical problem: posterior approximation degradation on out-of-distribution data in amortized Bayesian inference
Solid theoretical justification: Propositions 1-4 rigorously establish strict properness of self-consistency losses regardless of p*(x)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four diverse case studies (normal means, air traffic, neuroscience, images) with appropriate gold-standard comparisons and thorough ablations
Strong and consistent empirical results: Dramatic improvements in robustness even with minimal unlabeled data (4 samples) and far beyond training distribution
Practical applicability: Maintains amortization benefits, requires no ground-truth parameters for unlabeled data, works with real data
Well-executed: Clear presentation, detailed reproducibility information, effective visualizations
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Self-consistency introduced by Schmitt et al. [39] for efficiency; main contribution is recognizing application to robustness, which is somewhat incremental
Missing direct empirical comparisons: Paper cites robustness methods [20, 40, 43, 44] but doesn't provide head-to-head experimental comparison, making it difficult to assess relative effectiveness

Theory-practice gap: Theoretical results establish strict properness but don't rigorously explain why self-consistency minimization improves OOD generalization; connection is intuitive but lacks formal analysis

Unlabeled data is semi-synthetic in most experiments: Only air traffic uses substantial real data; MNIST uses synthetic misspecification; normal means uses prior-sampled data. Critical question unanswered: how does method perform when unlabeled data diverges significantly from both p(θ,x) and test distribution?
Restricted applicability: Method limited to normalizing flows requiring fast density evaluation; doesn't work with increasingly popular methods like flow matching and score-based diffusion
Incomplete hyperparameter and computational analysis: No guidance on choosing λ, sensitivity to p_C(θ) selection, computational overhead, or how much unlabeled data saturates benefits

Some experimental results show continued degradation even with method: Higher dimensionality (100D) shows larger bias; at least one country in air traffic case still performs poorly; estimated likelihood case notably worse than analytical

strengths: Addresses important problem of out-of-distribution robustness in ABI with practical relevance
Substantial empirical improvements demonstrated consistently across four diverse case studies (normal means, air traffic, Hodgkin-Huxley, MNIST)
Solid theoretical foundation with Propositions 1-3 establishing strict properness of self-consistency losses and showing no trade-offs with simulation-based objectives
Comprehensive experimental documentation with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Simple, practical method that can be integrated into existing ABI approaches
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies existing self-consistency losses from prior work [39] to a new domain rather than introducing new methodology
Critical missing baseline comparisons: no experimental evaluation against competing robustness methods [20, 40, 43], making it impossible to assess true merit relative to alternatives
Significant theory-practice gap: Proposition 4 shows strict properness fails for estimated likelihoods, yet experiments use estimated likelihoods without theoretical justification
Understated practical limitations: requires access to unlabeled real data during training (contradicting ABI's appeal), but implications not sufficiently discussed
Insufficient analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity: choice of p_C(θ) and λ acknowledged as difficult to anticipate but no ablations or guidance provided for practitioners

Incomplete experimental analysis: missing failure mode investigation (e.g., Ireland in air traffic), sensitivity to amount of unlabeled data, computational cost comparisons, and scaling to higher dimensions
Theory-empirics disconnect: Proposition 3 guarantees hold for any p*(x), but practical performance degradation with distribution mismatch is not investigated
Limited investigation of when/why method works: intuition for why self-consistency improves OOD robustness could be clearer, and conditions for success not well characterized

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: Poor robustness of ABI to out-of-distribution data limits real-world deployment; this work provides effective solution
Strong theoretical foundation: Rigorous proofs of strict properness (Propositions 1-4) provide theoretical justification; Proposition 3 elegantly shows no trade-off between loss components
Simple and practical solution: Easy to implement, maintains amortized inference speed, requires no ground-truth parameters for unlabeled data, compatible with any data source

Comprehensive experimental validation: Diverse case studies (toy problems, time series, neuroscience, images), systematic ablations, convincing results showing robustness far beyond training distribution
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear writing, well-organized, comprehensive appendix with implementation details, effective visualizations
Demonstrated effectiveness with minimal unlabeled data: Shows robustness gains with as few as 4 unlabeled observations, works with estimated likelihoods and high-dimensional data
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty: Self-consistency losses introduced in prior work (refs 26, 39); main contribution is application to robustness via semi-supervised learning rather than new methodology

Limited comparison with competing methods: Primary comparisons against vanilla NPE; lacks direct quantitative benchmarks against other robustness-enhancement approaches (post-hoc corrections, adversarial defenses, etc.)

Practical limitations underexplored: Density evaluation requirement limits applicability to certain architectures (acknowledged for flow matching/score-based methods but not deeply analyzed); guidance for hyperparameter selection (p_C(θ), λ) limited; failure modes not discussed

Weaker theoretical guarantees for estimated likelihood: Proposition 4 shows strict properness doesn't hold when both posterior and likelihood are unknown; theoretical understanding incomplete for the general case despite good empirical results
Missing computational cost analysis: Training time overhead of self-consistency loss not quantified; only inference speed discussed; computational comparisons absent

Limited statistical rigor: No formal significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values for claims; ablation studies on key design choices (L samples for variance, λ weighting, activation schedule) missing

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine robustness limitations of ABI with compelling examples
Solid theoretical contributions showing self-consistency losses are strictly proper and target the true posterior without trade-offs
Novel semi-supervised application extending self-consistency from simulation efficiency to leveraging unlabeled data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (normal means, air traffic, neuroscience, images) demonstrating broad applicability
Practical effectiveness with dramatic robustness improvements using minimal unlabeled data (as few as 4 observations)
Excellent reproducibility standards with detailed appendices, hyperparameters, and promised code availability
Appropriate positioning relative to related robustness methods with helpful comparisons to regularization and domain adaptation approaches
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core self-consistency concept from prior work (Schmitt et al. 2024); extension to semi-supervised setting is somewhat incremental; theoretical propositions follow straightforwardly from strictly proper scoring rules

Critical theory-practice gaps: (1) Requires known likelihood p(x|θ), but Figure 7 shows significant performance degradation with estimated likelihood; (2) Theory assumes universal density estimators, not finite-capacity neural networks; (3) KL divergence connection uses second-order Taylor approximation

Inadequate failure mode analysis: limited investigation of when self-consistency helps/hurts; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter λ; estimated likelihood case shows substantial posterior SD bias without thorough discussion; no exploration of distribution shift between unlabeled and test data

Experimental limitations: small unlabeled datasets (M≤32 typical); in experiments with real data (air traffic, MNIST), unlabeled data comes from same distribution as test data; overstated robustness claims—results show improvements only within moderate ranges (μ_obs<5), not substantially beyond training range

Applicability constraints: requires fast density evaluation (excludes flow matching/diffusion models); hyperparameter λ requires problem-specific tuning with limited guidance; choice of proposal p_C(θ) affects results but uninvestigated

Computational cost under-discussed: self-consistency requires posterior sampling and likelihood evaluation per training iteration; claims of competitive timing lack supporting evidence; no runtime comparisons with baselines provided

Incomplete experimental analysis: no formal statistical significance testing despite error bars; missing ablation studies on design choices; generalization to true out-of-distribution settings unclear; no analysis of minimum unlabeled data requirements or data quality diagnostics

Presentation issues: notation inconsistencies (x* meaning changes); key practical details relegated to appendix; unclear guidance on when practitioners should use this method; connection between variance and KL minimization could be clearer

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (synthetic, time series, dynamics, images) with detailed reproducibility information
Solid theoretical result that self-consistency losses are strictly proper and can be combined with simulation-based losses without trade-offs
Clear practical improvements demonstrated even with minimal unlabeled data (4 observations)
Honest discussion of method limitations (e.g., incompatibility with free-form flows)
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine robustness challenges in amortized Bayesian inference
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is relatively straightforward extension of existing SC losses (Schmitt et al. 2024) to unlabeled data

Theoretical results (Propositions 1-3) are standard applications of strict properness theory; no convergence rates, finite-sample analysis, or characterization of when SC improves robustness under misspecification

Misleading framing about model misspecification: claims SC targets 'analytic posterior' under misspecification, but this posterior is incorrect if the model is wrong; the paper does not adequately explain why enforcing a potentially incorrect Bayes' rule helps

Unfair baseline comparisons: UDA methods (NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD) compared with different data assumptions; they require large unlabeled datasets while NPE+SC is tested with ~4 samples, confounding two factors

Weak model misspecification demonstration: synthetic cases use artificial shifts (μ_prior mismatch), Hodgkin-Huxley uses same model, MNIST uses artificial prior misspecification; no cases with genuinely unknown model inadequacy
Proposition 4 admits strict properness fails with unknown likelihood, yet experiments show SC helps with estimated likelihood (Fig. 7)—this contradiction is underexplored
Practical limitations understated: method requires fast density evaluation (excludes major classes of flows), λ tuning required with schedules in high-d settings, no practical guidance provided
Missing ablations on λ sensitivity across problems and systematic investigation of unlabeled sample size effects
Code availability broken: abstract states URL but it is cut off, undermining reproducibility claims
Overclaiming: 'drastically improves' language exceeds empirical evidence in places

strengths: Well-motivated solution to a real problem in ABI: improving robustness to out-of-distribution queries without ground-truth parameters
Strong theoretical foundation: Propositions 1-3 rigorously establish strictly proper SC losses that target the analytical posterior with no trade-off against simulation-based losses
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (toy problems, time series, images) with extensive ablations on dimensionality, dataset size, and likelihood specification
Practical and accessible method: works with as few as 4 unlabeled observations, maintains amortization benefits, requires no post-hoc corrections
Solid reproducibility: code provided, detailed hyperparameters and architectures in appendices, complete proofs, hardware specifications
Clear presentation with good motivation and helpful visualizations (particularly Figure 1 demonstrating core contribution)
weaknesses: Significant performance degradation with estimated likelihoods (Figure 7 shows noticeable posterior SD bias and MMD increases)—this is the realistic case but receives limited analysis or solutions, substantially limiting practical applicability
Incremental novelty: self-consistency losses introduced by Schmitt et al. (2024) for supervised settings; main contribution is relatively straightforward extension to semi-supervised regime
Computational overhead not thoroughly characterized: requires fast density evaluations making flow matching and score-based diffusion impractical, but no timing comparisons or quantification provided

Limited analysis of failure modes and method boundaries: when should practitioners NOT use SC loss? What happens under extreme misspecification? Overselling Proposition 3's practical guarantees given estimated likelihood limitations

Hyperparameter tuning required: despite claims that λ lacks trade-offs, need for linear scheduling in high dimensions (Section 4.4) suggests sensitivity; limited guidance for practitioners on new problems
Real-world evaluation somewhat limited: air traffic uses only N=1024 simulations; MNIST denoising is artificial with known blur model; would benefit from more challenging authentic applications
Model misspecification discussion relegated to Appendix B despite being critical for understanding practical limitations with estimated likelihoods
